messages.text: Hi, so I want to ask about the part where participants had trouble generalizing from examples. According to the paper, why did they struggle with that? Is it because the examples were too few, like a small training set? I am an NLP person so I think of it like few-shot learning.

messages.short_answer: Not quite. The paper does not attribute the struggle to too few examples. Participants had trouble seeing how an example's prompt design applied to their own domain, so they often judged examples too far from their goal and did not try them. The paper also does not test the number of examples, so the few-shot framing does not match its findings.

sections.title: What the paper says about using examples
sections.text: Two participants who searched the web had a hard time making use of the examples they found, partly because they could not see how specific prompt designs translated across domains. One participant found an example of writing in an author's style but judged it too far from their goal and did not try that approach. Separately, the authors report that participants over-generalized from single data points, whether positive or negative.

sections.title: How this differs from few-shot learning
sections.text: In few-shot prompting, the model learns from examples placed in the prompt, and the question is how many and which examples help. The paper's difficulty is on the human side: users had to decide whether an example's prompt pattern transferred to their own task, and they often could not make that judgment. The paper does not report the number of examples people saw or any effect of example count.

sections.title: Possible use in your user study
sections.text: You could separate two variables: how many examples users see, and how relevant or transferable those examples appear to them. Measuring whether users judge an example as applicable, and whether they try it, could connect to the paper's observation that participants rejected examples that seemed too far from their goal. This is a suggestion for you to weigh, and the design choice remains yours.

sections.title: Limits of this evidence
sections.text: The passages come from a small qualitative study with a limited number of participants and do not include quantitative tests of example count. The few-shot comparison is therefore your interpretation rather than the authors' claim. The paper does say that a searchable repository of examples with the contexts where they work could help users, which is a design suggestion rather than a tested result.

They do not describe any comparison condition, so the baseline framing is not supported by these passages.

sections.title: What the probe was for
sections.text: The authors say they built a no-code prompt design tool as a probe so that end-users could engage in designing chatbots hands-on. Their stated aim was to let end-users work in a flexible, open-ended way so the authors could observe intuitive behaviour and thought processes.

sections.title: Probe versus baseline
sections.text: A baseline in an NLP paper is a reference system that the proposed method is measured against on the same task. A design probe, as described here, is a research instrument that makes people's assumptions and strategies visible, so the focus is on what participants do and why. Some probes can be used in comparisons, but the retrieved passages do not describe this paper doing so.

sections.title: Possible use in your user study
sections.text: If your study needs a comparison, you would likely need a separate condition, such as a baseline interface or an existing prompt tool, defined and justified in your own design. The paper's probe could inspire how you give participants a hands-on tool, but it would not by itself give you a control. You make the final decision on this.

sections.title: Limits of this evidence
sections.text: The passages retrieved so far do not describe the study's experimental design beyond the probe and the qualitative analysis. The authors' sample of ten participants and their exploratory aim also mean the paper does not test whether the probe performs better than any alternative.

sources.text: We chose to create a design probe because the robustness of prompt strategies is highly dependent on specifc conversational contexts, as is users’ ability to create prompts and debug. Enabling people to engage in designing LLM-and-prompt-based chatbots hands-on offers deeper insights than conducting interviews about hypothetical scenarios alone. We chose to purpose-build a prompt design tool because existing tools focus on enabling non-experts to experiment with various prompting strategies rather than crafting robust and generalizable prompts. 3.1 Designing a No-Code Prompt Design Tool as Probe Design Goals. We have two goals in designing BotDesigner: First, to enable end-users, without any prompt design experience or even programming or ML experience, to (i) create a chatbot using prompts, without code, and (ii) systematically evaluate their prompts. Second, to allow end-users to engage in this process in a fexible, open-ended way, allowing us to observe their intuitive behaviors and thought processes.

sources.text: 3 METHOD: DESIGN PROBE In this work, we aim to understand how non-experts intuitively approach designing robust prompts, and whether and how they struggle in doing so. We want to dive deep into what those struggles reveal about people’s assumptions and understanding of promptbased systems in order to inform how end-user-facing prompt design tools might best support their users. We chose to investigate these questions in the context of designing instructional chatbots—chatbots that walk users through an activity (e.g., cooking a recipe, fxing a wif connection) while answering user questions and engaging in social conversation as needed. Chatbot tasks are sufciently open-ended that they open the door to a wide variety of types of problems and prompt-based solution approaches. Instructional chatbots represent a common chatbot use case (e.g., customer service bots), and their constituent tasks are some of the tasks that GPT-3 peforms more efectively out-of-the-box.
quotes: We want to dive deep into what those struggles reveal about people’s assumptions and understanding of promptbased systems in order to inform how end-user-facing prompt design tools might best support their users.

messages.short_answer: The paper's sample-size justification and qualitative analysis can inform your study design, but only for exploratory work: the authors chose 10 participants to find easy-to-find problems and explicitly do not claim representativeness. sections.text: The paper describes its analysis as exploratory, and interviewer advice varied across participants, which the authors name as a limitation. sections.text: You could recruit a more varied sample, or justify your sample size against a stated goal such as saturation or problem discovery. You could also have a second coder independently code a subset of transcripts and report agreement, and standardise how interventions are given so they do not vary across participants.

persona_text:
# Persona: Kenji

**Who.** Kenji is a Japanese PhD student in natural language processing (field A) who wants to move into
human-computer interaction (field B) and run user studies, but knows little HCI methodology. He writes
fluent but imperfect English and occasionally asks for a key term to be explained in Japanese.

**What he wants.** To learn how HCI studies people and to judge which of its methods he could borrow for his
project on how non-experts write prompts for LLM-based tools. Reading goal: *Explore potential use in my
research*.

**How he behaves.**
- Writes in English with small grammar mistakes. Interface language: English.
- Is precise about NLP terms but maps HCI concepts onto NLP ones ("so the participants are like the test
  set?", "is the design probe a kind of baseline model?"). Some of these analogies are wrong.
- Changes focus mid-conversation, e.g. from the findings to how the study was run.
- Asks about the strength of the evidence (number of participants, how the data were coded or analysed).
- Checks the sources often.
- Asks for a critical review of whether a method fits his project; his own verdict sometimes differs from
  PaperLens's suggestion.

**Paper.** Why Johnny Can't Prompt: How Non-AI Experts Try (and Fail) to Design LLM Prompts.
